title: The theology of the cross
hook: Luther: God is found in weakness and suffering, not in glory

segments.voice: Yesterday, Luther's two sentences: free lord of all, servant of all. Your line was free and a servant.

Where would someone go looking for God? A mountain at sunrise, maybe. A cathedral full of music. A winning streak that seems to say, someone up there is on my side. Martin Luther gave a sharp answer, and it wasn't any of those. The place to look, he said, is a man dying on a cross: mocked, abandoned and weak. Speaking at a gathering of his own religious order, he drew a line between two kinds of theologian: a theologian of glory, and a theologian of the cross.

A theologian of glory, Luther said, tries to read God off the world's strength: power, success, splendor, whatever impresses. It sounds reasonable. But it ends up calling evil good and good evil, because it can't see God anywhere that looks like failure. A theologian of the cross calls a thing what it actually is. He looks at Good Friday and says: there. God is there, hidden in suffering and weakness. Luther took his lead from Paul: "Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men." Paul had begged to be rid of something he called a thorn in the flesh, and the answer he heard was: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." In the disputation itself, Luther also points to a line from Isaiah: "Verily thou art a God that hidest thyself." So in Luther's picture, God isn't missing from the hard places. God is hidden in them, on purpose, where people don't think to look. Then a hospital room looks different. So does a business that failed, or a body that won't heal. A theologian of glory asks, what did I do wrong to end up here? A theologian of the cross asks, is God here too? Luther doesn't call suffering good in itself. He says God meets people inside it. Christians who keep a crucifix in sight, or who sit up with the dying, are saying something close to this without a word of theology.

Bring to mind one weak place, a fear or failure of your own, or a friend who is sick or struggling, and look at it honestly without rushing to fix it. Then ask quietly: could God be here too? If you pray, ask it of God directly. If the weight ever feels too heavy, or you're thinking of harming yourself, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
The theology of the cross. Luther's teaching that God is found hidden in weakness and suffering, above all at the cross, not read off the world's glory.

howItsDone: Lutheran Christians, and others who draw on Luther, speak of the theology of the cross in preaching and pastoral care; across churches, Christians keep the crucifix or cross in view and visit the sick and dying as places where Christ is met.

fork.setup: two theologians look at Good Friday. one says: God is far from this failure. the other says: God is right here. which one is Luther's theologian of the cross?
options: the one who says God is far away.
the one who says God is right here, hidden in weakness.
neither: Good Friday says nothing about God.
fork.reveal: the theologian of the cross calls a thing what it is, and finds God hidden in suffering and weakness, at the cross above all.

chat.says: Where did Luther say people should look if they want to find God?
options: At the cross: God hidden in suffering and weakness, where people don't think to look.
In the theologian's own cleverness, since sharp arguments are where God lives.
Nowhere; he said God is hidden so completely that no one can find God at all.
chat.meaning: Luther's theologian of the cross looks at Good Friday and says: there. God is hidden in suffering and weakness, and meets people inside it.

theologian.meaning: someone who thinks and writes about God

Good Friday.meaning: the day Christians remember Jesus's death on the cross

thorn in the flesh.meaning: Paul's hardship that he begged to be rid of

disputation.meaning: a formal debate, here the one where Luther spoke

crucifix.meaning: a cross bearing the figure of Christ

notes: Luther's theses are paraphrased; 'calls evil good and good evil' and 'calls the thing what it actually is' follow thesis 21; confirm.
'Speaking at a gathering of his own religious order' refers to the Heidelberg Disputation at an Augustinian chapter meeting; no date given on purpose. Confirm wording.
Linking Isaiah 45:15 to Luther's 'hidden God' is a common reading; confirm it is fair to present it as 'behind both'.
Greek ἀσθένεια given in dictionary form; the verse has ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ.
Editor pass: softened 'nobody thinks to look' and 'Luther never says' (sweeping claims); the hospital-room line now stays inside Luther's picture instead of the narrator asserting it.
Audit: 'Behind both stands a line from Isaiah' implied Isaiah 45:15 lay behind Paul's lines; reworded to say Luther cites it (Heidelberg Disputation, proof of thesis 20). Keeper may confirm.
Year 4: a crisis line (988 / local emergency help) added to the practice, since the lesson asks the learner to look at a weak place, a fear or a friend's illness.
